summary: Defines an IRIS registry schema for registered DNS information, extending IRIS query and result operations to meet the needs of domain registries and registrars.

eli5.summary: It adds the question forms IRIS needs for the list of website names and who registered them.

questions: what is the dreg1 registry type
how does iris find a registry server
subtitle: The question and answer formats IRIS uses to look up domains, name servers, contacts and registrars.

tldr.problem: Domain registries and registrars need a standard way to answer lookups about domains, name servers, contacts and registration authorities, and the generic IRIS core protocol does not define those specifics.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3982 defines the dreg1 registry type as an XML Schema derived from IRIS. It adds six search queries, result types for domain, host, contact and registrationAuthority, privacy labels, and rules for finding servers.
tldr.outcome: A client can search registry data in a uniform way, and servers can mark data as private or denied rather than silently leaving it out. The RFC adds no new security considerations beyond IRIS itself.

today: RFC 3982 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the IRIS core protocol in RFC 3981.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) is a generic lookup protocol for registry data. IRIS requires each kind of registry to define its own query and result elements. RFC 3982 does that for Internet domain registries, as an XML Schema derived from and using the IRIS schema (RFC 3981). The registry type is called dreg1.

The queries and results are based on the functional requirements in the CRISP requirements document (RFC 3707). The schema is written with XML 1.0, XML Schema and XML Namespaces. Appendix A of the RFC gives examples of client and server exchanges.
sections.eli5: IRIS is a general way to ask a registry questions. This document fills in the details for the registry of website names.

sections.title: The Six Queries
sections.content:
The schema derives six search queries from the IRIS query element:

  • findRegistrarsByName searches for registrars, optionally restricted by baseDomain to those able to register subdomains in that domain. Its namePart can use beginsWith, endsWith or exactMatch. With no namePart it MUST return all applicable registrars.
  • findDomainsByContact finds domains through fields of a domain's contact, such as a contactHandle or the contact search group, and can be narrowed by a role.
  • findDomainsByName finds domains by their DNS name, with beginsWith and endsWith.
  • findDomainsByIDN works like the name query but considers internationalized domain names. It returns the domain and its variants, and its exactMatch MUST match only equivalent IDNs under RFC 3490.
  • findContacts searches for contacts using the contact search group.
  • findDomainsByHost finds domains hosted by a name server, given the host name, host handle, IPv4 address or IPv6 address.

The contact search group is shared by several queries. It can constrain by commonName, organization and eMail (exact address, or any address in a domain through inDomain, which MUST hold a valid domain name without an '@'). The city, region and postalCode elements accept only an exactMatch, with no substring searches. Several queries also take optional language elements, which are hints clients MAY send and servers MAY use, for example to tune normalization.
sections.eli5: There are six kinds of question: find a registrar, find a domain by who looks after it, by its name, by its international spelling, or by the server that hosts it, and find a contact person.

sections.title: The Four Result Types
sections.content:
Answers come back as one of four result types, which refer to each other with IRIS entity references.

  • domain represents a domain assignment. It carries the domainName (a name as in RFC 1035), an optional idn in nameprep form, a registry-unique domainHandle, nameServer references to hosts, a registrant and several kinds of contacts (billing, technical, administrative, legal, zone, abuse, security and other). It also carries status, registry and registrar references, and a set of timestamps such as initial delegation, last renewal and expiration.
  • host represents a name server registration, with hostHandle, hostName, ipV4Address, ipV6Address and hostContact.
  • contact represents a person, organization or role, with contactHandle, commonName, eMail, postalAddress, phone and fax, plus a language and translatedContacts pointing to equivalents in other languages.
  • registrationAuthority represents an entity that can register domains. Its role is given by a registry, registrar or other child, and its domain children name the domains it may register subdomains in.

A status element on a domain may hold at most one of each of eight values. On the registry and registrar references an optional boolean hosting attribute says the party answers DNS queries for the domain authoritatively. Phone numbers that start with '+' MUST follow E.164, and a country SHOULD be a two-letter ISO 3166 code.
sections.eli5: The answers come as four kinds of card: a card for a domain, one for the computer that serves it, one for a person to contact, and one for the company that can sell names.

sections.title: Privacy Labels
sections.content:
Some result values cannot be given out, but a client should still be told they exist or should be told not to pass them on. For these the schema uses special element types, such as dateTimePrivacyType, stringPrivacyType, domainStatusType and contactTypeType. These elements may be nil, meaning present but empty.

An element that is present without content MUST carry one or more of two boolean attributes: private (the content is absent because it may never be published) or denied (it is absent because policy does not allow it at the current level of access). An element that is present with content MAY carry doNotRedistribute (the content is not to be redistributed) or specialAccess (the content was provided because of special access rights).

These attributes SHOULD match the access level of the recipient. An anonymous or low-access user would expect private or denied, while an authenticated user with high access would expect doNotRedistribute or specialAccess.
sections.eli5: Some lines in the phone book are blacked out. The labels say whether a line is hidden for everyone or just for you, and whether you may copy the lines you were allowed to see.

sections.title: Finding the Right Server
sections.content:
The application service label for this registry type MUST be DREG1, the abbreviated form of the URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dreg1. Two alternative resolution methods are defined for IRIS URIs whose authority is only a domain name, without a port.

Bottom-up (identified as bottom) first tries IRIS direct resolution on the full name, such as example.com. If that yields no server that can be reached, it removes the leftmost label and tries again, such as com. If all labels are removed without a connection, DNS is queried for the address records of the original name and the well-known port for the default IRIS protocol is used.

Top-down (identified as top) starts at the rightmost label, which is always '.', and tries direct resolution. On failure it prepends the next label to the left, so '.' then com then example.com, and ends with the same DNS fallback.

The entity classes accepted by the IRIS lookupEntity query for this type are host-name, host-handle, domain-name, idn, domain-handle, contact-handle, ipv4-address, ipv6-address and registration-authority. Each yields a host, domain, contact or registrationAuthority result. The transport is BEEP, where this type uses the default message pattern and only basic TLS server authentication.
sections.eli5: To find who to ask, you either start with the full address and keep trimming words off the front until someone answers, or start from the biggest area and add words back.

sections.title: Internationalization
sections.content:
The type supports lookup of domain names in both traditional ASCII form and IDN form. Contact data may be non-ASCII and could contain almost any Unicode character, so queries that can touch such data take a language element. Clients should use it to name the target languages, and servers should use it to improve normalization and search.

Clients that localize the protocol need only localize the names of XML elements and attributes, plus elements with date and time information. The schema is designed so clients need not interpret other element or attribute content for localization. Date and time values in dateTimePrivacyType elements MUST use the 'Z' indicator for UTC. Results with possibly Unicode data come with language elements to help present them. If a client names a language the server does not support, the server MAY return the languageNotSupported error, listing the unsupported languages it was given. A server MAY also return searchTooWide when a query must be narrowed to fit its policies.
sections.eli5: Names and addresses can be written in any language, so questions can say which language you care about, and the server can say when it does not speak that one.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers three identifiers: the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dreg1, the S-NAPTR application service label DREG1, and the BEEP profile URI http://iana.org/beep/iris1/dreg1, in addition to the registration in the IRIS-BEEP document. The XML Schema in section 4 of the RFC is the formal definition.
sections.eli5: The document puts its name on the official list of names, so no one else uses the same label for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it lays out no new considerations for security precautions beyond those specified in the IRIS core protocol (RFC 3981). The privacy labels in section 3.2.1 are the registry type's own mechanism for flagging withheld or restricted data.
sections.eli5: This document adds no new safety rules. It follows the ones in the main IRIS rulebook.
